interest: This file offers historians an exceptional perspective on the multi-sided espionage and diplomatic maneuvering in neutral Afghanistan during World War II. It illustrates how the Afghan government adroitly balanced relations with Japan, Great Britain, and the Soviet Union, welcoming Japanese commercial penetration, engineers, and educational scholarships during the 1930s as a vital counterpoise against British hegemony and Soviet encirclement. Crucially, the records illuminate the Japanese Empire's efforts to project itself as a Pan-Islamic champion, its intelligence surveillance of Central Asia and Sinkiang, and its overtures offering arms and a partition of British India. Finally, the debriefings of returning Afghan exchange students provide rare, firsthand neutral testimonies regarding conditions inside wartime Japan, documenting extreme news fabrications around naval battles such as Guadalcanal, public despondency, and the widespread arrests of dissident scientists, professors, and intellectuals.
overview: This file comprises State Department records from decimal classification 894.20290H covering Japanese activities, espionage, intelligence operations, and propaganda in Afghanistan between late 1942 and early 1944. Initiated by Secretary of State Cordell Hull’s inquiry into reports of Japanese propaganda dissemination, the correspondence is anchored by extensive reporting from Cornelius Van H. Engert, U.S. Minister at Kabul. Engert provides deep historical and strategic assessments of Afghan–Japanese relations since the 1930s, analyzing Kabul’s policy of utilizing Tokyo as a diplomatic and commercial counterweight against Soviet penetration and British influence. The file tracks the limited Japanese presence in Afghanistan (approximately twenty-one legation staff and public works engineers), surveillance of engineer Genji Kobayashi's irrigation work in Kandahar and the subsequent departure of Japanese engineers via the Soviet Union, Japanese Pan-Asiatic and anti-Bolshevik propaganda themes, Axis proposals to partition India or deliver arms, and the return and debriefing of Afghan exchange students who observed wartime domestic conditions and totalitarian press controls inside Japan.

subfiles.about: Internal State Department routing and charge slip logging file movements between August and December 1942.
subfiles.from: Department of State filing clerks
subfiles.summary: This record logs the internal circulation and charging out of decimal file 894.20290H to departmental officers, including John Carter Vincent and the Division of Far Eastern Affairs. It tracks corrections and cross-references between August 25, 1942, and December 22, 1942.
subfiles.title: Charge Slip for File 894.20290H
subfiles.to: PD Vincent, NCR Ford, Division of Far Eastern Affairs

subfiles.about: State Department request for an intelligence report regarding Japanese personnel, activities, and influence in Afghanistan.
subfiles.from: Cordell Hull (Secretary of State, Washington)
subfiles.summary: Following intimations from an interested U.S. government agency that Japan is attempting to disseminate propaganda in and from Afghanistan, Secretary Hull instructs the Legation at Kabul to report promptly. The inquiry requests specific information on the total number of Japanese nationals in the country, the nature of their interests and operations, and the extent of their influence with the Afghan government.
subfiles.title: Telegram from Hull to American Legation, Kabul, Requesting Report on Japanese Activities

subfiles.about: Historical background on Afghan-Japanese diplomatic, economic, and educational ties as a counterweight against the Soviet Union.
subfiles.from: Cornelius Van H. Engert (Kabul via New Delhi)
subfiles.summary: Engert reviews the history of Afghan–Japanese relations since the 1931 Treaty of Friendship, explaining that Kabul fostered relations with Tokyo primarily as a diplomatic counterpoise against Moscow. He notes King Nadir Shah's impressions of Japan's defiance of the League of Nations and the West in 1931, the mandate that Kabul's 1933 radio installation include direct communications with Tokyo, and the dispatch of Afghan students to Japan in 1935. Economically, Japanese imports of artificial silk and chinaware successfully challenged Russian and Indian commercial penetration prior to 1939.
subfiles.title: Telegram No. 74 (Section One) from Engert on Afghan-Japanese Diplomatic and Commercial Background

subfiles.about: Japanese intelligence collection focused on Soviet Central Asia and India, and propaganda concerning Moslem unrest in Sinkiang.
subfiles.from: Cornelius Van H. Engert / Norris S. Haselton (Kabul via New Delhi)
subfiles.summary: Engert explains that the Japanese Legation in Kabul evolved into a crucial political and intelligence outpost monitoring Soviet policy in Central Asia and British vulnerabilities in India. He details Japanese and German exploitation of Afghan sympathies for the Moslem Tungan uprising in Chinese Sinkiang, including clandestine travel of Japanese agents and anti-Soviet propaganda subsidies. He also reports that the Legation subsidized Kabul newspapers, staged a high-profile conversion of a Japanese mission member to Islam in 1934, and cultivated the Hazara population.
subfiles.title: Telegram No. 74 (Section Two) from Engert/Haselton on Japanese Espionage and Sinkiang

subfiles.about: Detailed analysis of Japanese wartime propaganda themes in Kabul and the deep-seated Afghan skepticism toward Tokyo.
subfiles.from: Cornelius Van H. Engert (Kabul via New Delhi)
subfiles.summary: This section delineates four primary Japanese propaganda arguments: claiming racial solidarity and protection for Asian Moslems against British imperialism; preaching an irresistible New Order; championing anti-Communism; and falsely claiming native officials in occupied lands like the Philippines were retained at higher pay. Engert reports that Afghan elites view Japanese pretensions with suspicion and distaste, associating them with Hindu domination and remaining annoyed by Japanese diplomatic tactlessness. However, the Japanese anti-Bolshevik message retains weight due to universal Afghan hatred and dread of Soviet doctrines.
subfiles.title: Telegram No. 74 (Section Three) from Engert on Japanese Propaganda Themes and Afghan Elite Reactions

subfiles.about: Census and intelligence activities of Japanese nationals in Afghanistan and the reasons for their non-expulsion.
subfiles.from: Cornelius Van H. Engert / Norris S. Haselton (Kabul via New Delhi)
subfiles.summary: Engert reports that only 21 Japanese subjects reside in Afghanistan, consisting of 16 legation personnel and families (noting the Chargé d'Affaires has a Scottish wife) and 5 public works department employees. Several staff members are former army officers speaking Persian who run intelligence networks via native travelers and truck drivers into Russia, Iran, and India. He explains that Japanese nationals were not expelled alongside German and Italian nationals in 1941 because of Japanese neutrality at the time and Soviet diplomatic complications, concluding that Afghans harbor intense dread of postwar Russian aggression.
subfiles.title: Telegram No. 74 (Section Four, Corrected Copy) from Engert/Haselton on Japanese Residents in Afghanistan

subfiles.about: Original transmitted text of Telegram 74, Section Four, showing internal State Department strikethroughs regarding British and Russian policy.
subfiles.from: Cornelius Van H. Engert / Norris S. Haselton (Kabul via New Delhi)
subfiles.summary: This document is the uncorrected text of Section Four of Telegram 74 as decoded in Washington. It includes penciled strikethroughs over paragraph 8, which explains why the British and Soviet governments did not insist on expelling Japanese nationals along with Italian and German nationals in late 1941. It records identical intelligence concerning the 21 Japanese nationals and Afghan anxieties over Soviet expansionism.
subfiles.title: Telegram No. 74 (Section Four, Original Received Copy) from Engert/Haselton with Editorial Deletions

subfiles.about: Notification that Japanese engineer Genji Kobayashi was dispatched to Kandahar Province to work on the Boghra irrigation canal.
subfiles.from: Cornelius Van H. Engert (American Legation, Kabul)
subfiles.summary: Engert reports that Mr. Genji Kobayashi, one of the Japanese engineers employed by the Afghan Ministry of Public Works who had been recalled to Kabul earlier in the year, departed on October 18, 1942, for Girishk in Kandahar Province. Kobayashi was assigned to resume engineering work on the Boghra irrigation canal until May 1943. Engert notes that the British Legation in Kabul made no objection to Kobayashi’s presence in the interior.
subfiles.title: Despatch No. 54 from Engert on Japanese Engineer Assigned to Kandahar Province

subfiles.about: Routine interagency transmittal of Despatch No. 54 regarding Japanese engineering and intelligence movements.
subfiles.from: Department of State (Division of Far Eastern Affairs / FC)
subfiles.summary: A formal transmittal form through which the Department of State disseminates copies of Engert’s strictly confidential Despatch No. 54 of November 13, 1942, to U.S. wartime intelligence organizations: the Military Intelligence Service, the Office of Naval Intelligence, the Federal Bureau of Investigation, and the Office of Strategic Services.
subfiles.title: State Department Transmission Slip Routing Despatch No. 54 to Intelligence Agencies
subfiles.to: Military Intelligence Service (MIS), Office of Naval Intelligence (ONI), FBI, Office of Strategic Services (OSS)

subfiles.about: Japanese offers of student scholarships, trade, and war matériel, alongside escalated propaganda denouncing American imperialism.
subfiles.from: Cornelius Van H. Engert (Kabul via New Delhi)
subfiles.summary: Engert reports confidential disclosures that the Japanese Minister offered to fund more Afghan students in Japan, conclude a trade treaty, and supply war matériel via Russia. Following German reverses at Stalingrad, Japanese propaganda intensified, portraying American war production and Pacific victories as fabrications, citing Pearl Harbor, and attacking William Phillips's mission to India as proof of predatory U.S. imperialism. Japanese diplomats also dangled territorial incentives, suggesting sympathy for Afghanistan's ambition for an ocean port and suggesting Afghanistan and Japan partition India, while quietly distancing themselves from Germany's failing European campaign.
subfiles.title: Telegram No. 44 from Engert on Japanese Proposals and Anti-American Propaganda Campaign

subfiles.about: Arrival in Kabul of three Afghan exchange students educated in Tokyo and their political impressions.
subfiles.from: Cornelius Van H. Engert (Kabul via New Delhi)
subfiles.summary: Engert reports the return of three Afghan students who had studied in Japan since 1936 under Japanese Foreign Office sponsorship. One student received an audience with the King, asserting that Japan could never be defeated due to resources seized in Malaya and the Dutch East Indies and portraying Japan as a great Islamic champion poised to liberate Asia and check Soviet expansion into Persia and Afghanistan. Engert notes that while former minister Habibullah Tarzi shares pro-Japanese sentiments, most Afghans dislike the Japanese and fear potential Japanese ties with the Indian National Congress.
subfiles.title: Telegram No. 82 from Engert on Return of Afghan Students from Japan

subfiles.about: Administrative transfer of document 894.20290H/9 to decimal file 811.42790H.

subfiles.summary: A State Department transfer sheet recording that confidential document 894.20290H/9 has been transferred to decimal file 811.42790H.
subfiles.title: Cross-Reference Sheet Transferring Document 894.20290H/9

subfiles.about: Detailed biographical data on the three Afghan students returning from Japan, focusing on Abdullah Khan.
subfiles.from: Cornelius Van H. Engert (American Legation, Kabul)
subfiles.summary: Confirming Telegram No. 82, Engert names the three returned students: Abdullah Khan, Ghulam Naqshband Khan, and Abdul Hakim Khan, who studied under Japanese Cultural Relations sponsorship. He provides biographical background on Abdullah Khan, whose father Mirza Mohamed Khan was a prominent cabinet minister and diplomat, and whose sister married Amir Habibullah. Engert cautions that Abdullah Khan has a questionable reputation and is suspected of harboring pro-Amanullah sympathies.
subfiles.title: Despatch No. 153 from Engert Identifying Three Returned Afghan Students

subfiles.about: Debriefing of returned student Abdul Hakim Khan regarding strict censorship, military fabrications, and persecution of intellectuals in Japan.
subfiles.from: Cornelius Van H. Engert (American Legation, Kabul)
subfiles.summary: Engert reports that returned student Abdul Hakim Khan expressed starkly different, unvarnished views of wartime Japan compared to Abdullah Khan. Hakim stated that the Japanese public was kept in total ignorance of military setbacks, recounting how the broadcast of a Japanese cruiser sinking off Guadalcanal caused such popular depression that state radio immediately fabricated the sinking of three American cruisers. He further reported that educated elites, professors, scientists, and writers were fully aware Japan would lose the war and were being arrested in large numbers.
subfiles.title: Despatch No. 166 from Engert on Abdul Hakim Khan’s Impressions of Japan

subfiles.about: Cross-reference to Despatch No. 228 transmitting names of Japanese engineers employed by the Afghan government.
subfiles.from: Cornelius Van H. Engert (American Legation, Kabul)
subfiles.summary: A State Department cross-reference file sheet indexing Despatch No. 228 of July 10, 1943, from Engert at Kabul, filed originally under 862.20290h/18. The document transmits the specific names of Japanese engineers employed in the Afghan Government service.
subfiles.title: Cross-Reference Sheet for Despatch No. 228 on Japanese Engineers

subfiles.about: Cross-reference to Despatch No. 263 transmitting Afghan reactions to Japanese propaganda in India and Burma.
subfiles.from: Charles W. Thayer (American Legation, Kabul)
subfiles.summary: A State Department cross-reference sheet referencing Despatch No. 263, dated August 19, 1943, sent by Charles W. Thayer from Kabul and filed under 894.202450/2. The despatch reports on Afghan official and public reactions to Japanese wartime propaganda campaigns across India and Burma.
subfiles.title: Cross-Reference Sheet for Despatch No. 263 on Propaganda in India and Burma

subfiles.about: Evacuation of four Japanese engineers from Kabul to Japan via Soviet territory at Termez.
subfiles.from: Cornelius Van H. Engert (Kabul)
subfiles.summary: Engert notifies the State Department that the four Japanese engineers previously employed by the Afghan government departed Kabul for Japan via Russia on September 24, 1943. They crossed the Soviet border at Termez on September 29. Engert requests that the American Embassy in Moscow be alerted to their transit.
subfiles.title: Telegram No. 179/197 from Engert on Departure of Japanese Engineers via Termez

subfiles.about: Clerical correction altering the transmission number of Engert's telegram from 179 to 197.
subfiles.from: State Department Telegraph / Communications Section
subfiles.summary: An administrative correction sheet directing that Telegram No. 179, dated October 13, 1943, regarding the departure of Japanese engineers through Russia, be renumbered and corrected on the original file copy as Telegram No. 197.
subfiles.title: Departmental Correction Slip for Telegram No. 179

subfiles.about: Arrival in Kabul of two more Afghan exchange students from Japan and press censorship regarding their place of study.
subfiles.from: Cornelius Van H. Engert (American Legation, Kabul)
subfiles.summary: Engert reports the return to Kabul via Siberia of two additional Afghan exchange students: Abdullah Khan Rahimi (who studied mining engineering) and Nur Ahmad Khan (who studied painting, metal engraving, and printing). He highlights an article in the Kabul newspaper Islah of January 20, 1944, which reported their educational achievements but deliberately and discreetly omitted any mention of Japan as the country of study. Engert notes the Legation's efforts to discreetly interview the men through third parties.
subfiles.title: Despatch No. 380 from Engert on Return of Afghan Students Rahimi and Nur Ahmad Khan
